content: Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS) is a rare and severe condition characterized by thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (destruction of red blood cells due to small blood vessel damage), and acute kidney injury. The primary cause of aHUS is dysregulation of complement regulatory proteins, which can be either inherited or acquired. Approximately 40% of affected individuals are under the age of 18. Historically, aHUS often resulted in kidney failure or death, but advancements in understanding the disease have led to the development of novel therapeutic options. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and risks of various interventions for aHUS. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Register of Studies, which includes data from CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, conference proceedings, the International Clinical Trials Register (ICTRP) Search Portal, and ClinicalTrials.gov. The search included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) up to September 3, 2020, as well as non-randomized studies up to July 27, 2020. Given the rarity of aHUS, prospective single-arm studies were also included in the analysis. The review included all randomized and non-randomized clinical trials that compared an intervention with either a placebo, supportive therapy, or another intervention. Due to the limited availability of RCTs for this rare condition, single-arm studies were also considered. Two independent authors extracted pre-specified data from eligible studies and assessed the risk of bias using a newly developed tool based on Cochrane criteria. Since statistical meta-analysis was not feasible, a qualitative analysis of the data was performed. Five single-arm studies were included in the review, all of which investigated the use of terminal complement inhibitors for the treatment of aHUS. Four studies focused on eculizumab, a short-acting C5 inhibitor, while one study evaluated ravulizumab, a longer-acting C5 inhibitor. All studies were non-randomized and single-arm in design, which introduced a high risk of bias and limited the ability to draw definitive conclusions from the evidence. The studies on eculizumab included data from 100 patients across three primary studies, with additional data from 37 patients in a secondary study. The ravulizumab study included 58 patients. After 26 weeks of eculizumab therapy, no deaths were reported, and there was a 70% reduction in the number of patients requiring dialysis. A complete thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) response was observed in 60% of patients at 26 weeks and in 65% of patients at two years. In the ravulizumab study, after 26 weeks of therapy, four patients (7%) had died, and a complete TMA response was observed in 54% of patients. Both eculizumab and ravulizumab were associated with significant improvements in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and health-related quality of life. However, serious adverse events were reported in 42% of patients across the studies. Notably, two cases of meningococcal infection occurred, both in patients treated with eculizumab. The authors concluded that terminal complement inhibition appears to provide favorable outcomes for patients with aHUS when compared to historical data. However, the evidence is of very low quality due to the reliance on non-randomized, single-arm studies. Conducting RCTs in aHUS is unlikely due to the rarity of the condition. Therefore, future research should focus on carefully analyzing additional single-arm studies and long-term follow-up data to better understand the optimal duration of treatment, potential adverse effects, and the risk of disease recurrence associated with terminal complement inhibition.
